Copper press fittings for CTS tube, joined with a jaw-compressed sleeve and an EPDM O-ring instead of solder. No flame, no flux, no draining the line dry — which is why press has taken over occupied-building and retrofit work.

Sizes run 1/2" through 2" and larger, in press x press, press x FTG, press x FIP and press x MIP. Fitting bodies are copper with brass used where the fitting transitions to thread. Tees, reducing tees, couplings, unions and reducers make up most of the range, with reducing tees the largest single group.

Two rules decide whether a press joint holds. The tube must be fully inserted to the depth mark — a shallow insertion presses but does not seal. And the system is proprietary: Viega and Mueller profiles are pressed by different jaws, so buy the fitting that matches your tool, not the cheaper one.

Sizing a run? Our press fitting technical specifications cover copper tube dimensions per ASTM B88, seal compounds by service, ASME B16.51 and jaw compatibility — and our copper pipe and tube specifications cover Type K, L and M walls and which type your code requires.

Carbon steel press fittings for fuel gas, pressed with a jaw tool and sealed with an HNBR O-ring rated for gas service. Sizes 1/2" through 2", in press, press x FTG, press x FIP, press x MIP and press x flange.

The advantage over threading is time and access: no cutting oil, no die head, no rotating the pipe, and the joint is complete in seconds. On a live building or a tight mechanical room, that difference is the whole reason to specify it.

The O-ring compound is what makes these gas-specific. The yellow HNBR seal used here is not the black EPDM used on water press fittings, and the two must never be substituted — EPDM degrades in hydrocarbons. Confirm the fitting is marked for gas before installing.

Systems are proprietary. Viega and Mueller press profiles require their own jaws, so match the fitting brand to your tool.

PureFlow presses a stainless sleeve over the fitting with a jaw tool. Unlike crimp, the connection can be verified visually — the Smart Connect feature deliberately leaks at low pressure if the fitting was not pressed, so an unpressed joint is found during the pressure test rather than after the wall closes.

Polymer bodies are worth choosing where water is aggressive. Brass dezincifies in acidic or high-chloride supply over years of service; the polymer version is dimensionally identical and immune to it. Zero Lead brass covers everything potable.

The range runs reducing tees, 90° elbows, couplings, reducing couplings and adapters, with reducing tees the deepest group.

F1960 cold expansion fittings for PEX-A. The tubing and its ring are stretched with an expander tool, the fitting is inserted, and the tubing's shape memory shrinks it back down onto the barb. No crimp ring to check with a gauge and no insert restricting the bore.

The method works only with PEX-A. PEX-B and PEX-C do not have enough shape memory to recover and will not seal on an expansion fitting, so confirm the tubing grade before ordering.

Sizes run 1/2" through 1-1/4" including reducing configurations. Bodies come in composite (poly) and brass, plus DZR forged brass. The composite versions are worth specifying where water is acidic or high in chlorides, since ordinary brass dezincifies under those conditions; they also cost less and resist freezing better.

Also stocked: sweat, male and female adapters for transitions to copper and threaded systems.

Gruvlok grooved mechanical fittings and couplings for fire protection, HVAC and industrial piping. Sizes 2" through 12", in painted carbon steel, galvanized, 304 and 316 stainless.

A grooved joint is made by rolling or cutting a groove near the pipe end, seating a gasket over the gap and bolting a two-piece housing around it. It goes together far faster than welding or flanging on large diameters, needs no hot work permit, and can be taken apart for service — which is why it dominates riser and mechanical-room piping.

Rigid and flexible couplings are not the same product. Flexible couplings allow angular deflection and absorb thermal movement and vibration; rigid couplings do not and are required where the system must behave as a solid assembly. Mixing them incorrectly shows up as noise and stressed joints.

Gasket compound must match the medium and temperature. EPDM (green) is the standard for water and is not suitable for petroleum service.

Black malleable iron threaded fittings for gas, steam, compressed air and hydronic heating. Sizes 1/8" through 4", in FIP, MPT x FPT, three-way FPT and flanged configurations.

Black iron is used on gas because it carries no zinc. Zinc coating can shed inside a fuel gas line and the flakes foul controls and orifices downstream, which is why black is the trade default even though a galvanized fitting looks identical on the shelf. NFPA 54 does permit galvanized steel pipe for fuel gas, so the requirement on any given job comes from the local code and the gas utility rather than from a blanket ban.

Threads are NPT and taper — the seal comes from thread deformation, not from the sealant, so the correct engagement depth matters more than how much dope is applied. Use a sealant rated for the medium: standard pipe dope is not approved for gas, where a yellow gas-rated PTFE tape or a listed compound is required.

Tees, couplings, 90° elbows and street elbows, bushings, caps and plugs make up the range.

Predominantly Mueller Streamline.

Galvanized malleable iron fittings in 1/8" through 4", threaded NPT. Tees, couplings, bushings, 90° elbows, street and adapter elbows, and plugs, in FIP, MPT x FPT, three-way FPT and flanged patterns.

These are the same malleable iron castings used in black iron, finished with a hot-dip zinc coating. That coating is the whole difference: it buys external corrosion resistance for damp, exposed and outdoor runs, at the cost of internal flaking over long service life.

Do not use galvanized on interior fuel gas. Zinc shed from the coating travels downstream and fouls regulators, valves and burner orifices, and most codes prohibit it outright — black iron is the material for gas.

Where galvanized meets copper, install a dielectric union. The two metals in contact with water between them form a galvanic cell, and the steel side corrodes through at the joint well before either pipe reaches its normal service life.

Brass threaded fittings for potable water, air and general service. Sizes 1/8" through 2" and larger, in FIP, FIP x MIP and MIP patterns, with AWWA thread available for water service work.

Brass is chosen over steel here for corrosion resistance and machinability rather than strength, and over plastic where the joint has to be taken apart repeatedly or exposed to heat. Anything installed on a potable line must be lead-free under federal law, so check the marking — the visual difference between lead-free and legacy brass is nil.

Dezincification is the failure mode to design against. In acidic or high-chloride water, zinc leaches out of ordinary brass over years and leaves a porous copper structure that eventually fails under pressure. DZR (dezincification-resistant) alloy solves it and is worth specifying where local water is known to be aggressive.

ABS DWV fittings for drain, waste and vent. Sizes 1-1/2" through 6", in all-hub, hub x hub, hub x spigot and threaded configurations.

ABS joins with a one-step solvent cement — no primer, unlike PVC — which makes it faster in cold conditions and is part of why it remains standard in much of the western U.S. and Canada. The cement is not interchangeable with PVC cement, and transition cement is required where the two materials meet.

Sanitary tees, wyes, tee-wye combinations, double configurations and closet flanges make up most of the range. The distinction between a sanitary tee and a wye matters at inspection: a sanitary tee is only permitted where flow changes from horizontal to vertical, never from vertical to horizontal, where a long-sweep wye is required.

ABS is not UV stable. Anything exposed outdoors needs paint or a different material.

PVC DWV fittings for drain, waste and vent. Sizes 1-1/2" through 8", in all-hub, hub x hub, hub x spigot and threaded configurations, plus PVC no-hub for cast iron transitions.

DWV fittings are not pressure rated. They carry ASTM D 2665 and are dimensionally similar to Schedule 40 pressure fittings, which is exactly why they get used by mistake — check the print rather than the shape before putting one on a supply line.

Joining requires primer and then cement on both surfaces, quarter-turned on assembly. Purple primer is not decoration: most inspectors look for the stain as proof the joint was primed, and its absence is a common failure even on sound work.

The range covers wyes, sanitary tees, tee-wye combinations, 45° elbows, flush bushings and closet flanges. As with ABS, a sanitary tee is only permitted on a horizontal-to-vertical transition.

Frequently asked questions

What does a backwater valve do?

A backwater valve lets wastewater flow out of the building but closes if the sewer backs up, so sewage cannot come back in through floor drains and low fixtures. Match the valve to the pipe size and material, such as 2" ABS.

Why support an expansion tank with a bracket?

A thermal expansion tank full of water is heavy, and hanging it from the water heater piping puts that weight on the fittings. A bracket such as the Sioux Chief 598-023 carries the tank so the piping does not have to.

F1807 crimp or F1960 expansion PEX fittings?

They are different systems with different tools. F1807 fittings are crimped with a copper or stainless ring; F1960 fittings need expansion PEX tubing and an expansion tool. Match the fitting to the system already installed. See F1807 crimp fittings.
